summary.text: A hydrogen bond forms when a hydrogen atom attached to a more electronegative atom interacts with another electronegative atom that bears a lone pair of electrons.
Its strength ranges from 4.2 to 167.4 kJ/mol, which makes it stronger than van der Waals interactions but generally weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.
It is responsible for the anomalously high boiling point of water and for stabilising protein and nucleic acid structures.

facts.label: Written as
facts.value: Dn−H···Ac, with the dots marking the hydrogen bond

facts.label: Typical donors
facts.value: A protic hydrogen on nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine

items.prompt: A student ranks three attractions from weakest to strongest: the pull between nonpolar neighbours (van der Waals), a hydrogen bond, and a covalent bond. Which ranking is right?

options.label: van der Waals, then hydrogen bond, then covalent bond
hydrogen bond, then van der Waals, then covalent bond
covalent bond, then hydrogen bond, then van der Waals
hydrogen bond, then covalent bond, then van der Waals

items.explain: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than van der Waals interactions but generally weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.

items.prompt: Two water molecules attract. The O–H hydrogen of one points at a lone pair on the oxygen of the other. Which atom plays the acceptor role?

options.label: The hydrogen atom that is bound to the first oxygen
The oxygen with the lone pair, on the second molecule
The oxygen that the hydrogen is already bound to
Both oxygens equally, since they are identical atoms

items.explain: The acceptor carries the lone pair and is not covalently attached to the hydrogen; the atom the hydrogen is bound to is the donor.

items.prompt: Water boils unusually high for its kind of compound, and proteins keep their folded structures. Which interaction do chemists credit for both?

options.label: Ionic bonds that join neighbouring molecules together
Covalent bonds that tie each protein into one rigid piece
Gravity pulling the molecules toward one another
Hydrogen bonding, an attraction that involves hydrogen

items.explain: Hydrogen bonding is responsible for water's anomalously high boiling point and for stabilising protein and nucleic acid structures.

items.prompt: In a crystal structure, the distance between a donor and an acceptor atom is smaller than the sum of their van der Waals radii. What can chemists take from that?

options.label: The two atoms must have formed a covalent bond
The two atoms are repelling each other strongly
It signals the strength of the hydrogen bond between them
Nothing, as distance says nothing about bond strength

items.explain: Donor–acceptor distances smaller than the sum of the van der Waals radii can be taken as an indication of hydrogen bond strength.

items.prompt: Hydrogen bonds usually involve nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, but a hydrogen on the carbon of chloroform can also take part. How do such carbon-based bonds compare?

options.label: They are weak and rare compared with the usual kind
They are stronger, because carbon forms so many bonds
They are identical, since the hydrogen is the same atom
They are stronger than covalent bonds, which makes them special

items.explain: Carbon can serve as a donor when it or a neighbour is electronegative, but hydrogen bonds involving C−H bonds are both very rare and weak.

items.prompt: A spectrometer shows that the stretching frequency of an X−H bond drops to lower energy when it takes part in a hydrogen bond. What does this shift reflect?

options.label: The X−H bond has become stiffer and stronger
The acceptor has lost its lone pair of electrons
The X−H bond has become weaker
The molecule has turned into an ionic compound

items.explain: Hydrogen bonding shifts the X−H stretching frequency to lower energy, which reflects a weakening of the X−H bond.
